title: Pancakes
subtitle: Thin British pancakes with lemon and sugar
excerpt: Classic thin British pancakes made from a simple batter of plain flour, eggs, and milk. Light and slightly golden, rolled up with lemon juice and caster sugar. Made for Shrove Tuesday and every other day.

recipe.sourceNotes: The British pancake is a thin, lacy crepe rather than the thick, fluffy American pancake. The oldest known British pancake recipe dates from 1439. Pancake Day, or Shrove Tuesday, is a tradition dating to the Middle Ages, when the eggs and butter used in the recipe needed to be used up before Lent. The batter should rest for at least 30 minutes so the starch grains in the flour absorb the liquid and the bubbles subside: rested batter makes a smoother, more even pancake.

content.text: Let the batter rest for at least 30 minutes: this gives a smoother, thinner pancake. The first pancake is usually a test: it tells you whether the pan is the right temperature and whether you have the right amount of batter per pancake. Swirl the batter immediately when it hits the pan to cover the base in a thin, even layer.

items.preparation: melted, plus extra for the pan

content.text: Whisk the flour, eggs, and a little of the milk together until smooth. Add the remaining milk gradually, whisking to avoid lumps. Stir in the melted butter and salt. Leave to rest for at least 30 minutes.

Heat a non-stick frying pan over medium-high heat. Add a small knob of butter and swirl to coat. Pour in a small ladleful of batter (about 80 ml) and swirl immediately so it covers the base in a thin layer.
Cook for 1 to 2 minutes until the edges are dry and the underside is golden. Flip with a palette knife or toss the pan. Cook for a further 30 seconds. Slide onto a plate.
Repeat with the remaining batter, stacking the pancakes on a plate. Serve with lemon juice squeezed over and a pinch of caster sugar.
